title: Tubular Ion Trapping & Transporter Saturation Biology
text: The physiological justification for urinary pH manipulation relies on the biophysical mechanism of non-ionic diffusion and ion trapping across the tubular epithelium. Lipid-soluble unionized molecules readily diffuse across the apical lipid bilayer of renal tubular cells back into the bloodstream. In the proximal tubule, apical sodium-hydrogen antiporters (NHE3) secrete protons into the lumen, acidifying the filtrate to pH 5.5. For a weak acid such as salicylate with pKa 3.0, administering sodium bicarbonate alkalinizes the tubular fluid to pH 8.0. Under this Henderson-Hasselbalch shift, over 99.9% of the drug becomes ionized into charged conjugate base anions that cannot penetrate the hydrophobic apical membrane. Furthermore, organic cation transporters such as OCT2 on the basolateral membrane and MATE1/MATE2-K on the apical membrane exhibit capacity-limited Michaelis-Menten kinetics; when plasma concentrations exceed their transporter binding affinity Km, active secretion saturates, limiting clearance. This cellular membrane transport biology governs renal excretion.
